summary.text: 工 is a whole-graph pictograph interpreted as a tool, though the exact object is disputed. The character is also attested in uses for occupations and work, but the evidence does not establish a single chronological path from the pictured tool to those meanings.

formation.text: Pictographic: early forms are described as tool-like. Analyses differ over whether the object is a bladed tool, perhaps also serving as a carpenter’s square, a square, or a building tool. These are interpretations of the whole graph, not established component analyses. The transmitted Shuowen account instead explains 工 as 巧飾, relating its form to a person with measuring tools; this is a historical explanation, not independent confirmation of the graph’s original referent.

components.text: 工 is treated here as one complete pictorial graph: its early form is interpreted as a tool, but the object’s identity is unsettled. It has no separately identified internal components.

history.text: The inspected paleographic account describes oracle-bone and bronze forms as tool-like and notes a thicker lower stroke in some early bronze forms. No inspectable, securely identified glyph image was available here, so no particular early graphic sequence can be traced.
A transmitted Shuowen account records 𢒄, containing 彡, as an ancient form of 工. The evidence does not establish whether this graph is an ancestor, a variant, or otherwise related to 工.

uncertainties.text: The graph’s proposed object remains disputed; the object’s name and pronunciation are not established, and 工’s own reconstructed readings do not identify it. The cited early artifact examples are not dated in the inspected account, so they do not establish the earliest attestation of each use.

The evidence does not establish whether early official or status uses are semantically related to craft and work uses, nor a chronological chain from the proposed tool image through skilled work to achievement. 工 is also reported as a whole-graph loan for 貢 in oracle-bone contexts; the borrowing sound comparison and dates are not established here.

senses.text: The graph is interpreted as picturing a tool, but the precise object is disputed. The cited evidence does not date the relevant artifacts, so this is not a securely dated earliest word meaning.
Oracle-bone examples are reported with 工 used as a state or place name; the displayed evidence does not date them or connect this use to the proposed tool meaning.

senses.gloss: official title, status, or occupation term
senses.period: oracle-bone and bronze examples; dating unresolved
senses.text: Reported examples use 工 for status or occupation and in official titles. Their relationship to the craft and work senses is not established.

senses.period: early examples and received Zhouli tradition; dating unresolved
senses.text: Examples are reported for craft workers, including 百工; the received Zhouli tradition also uses 工 for skilled makers. These attestations do not establish when this sense began or how it relates to the tool interpretation.
Work and labor are current senses. The evidence gives no dated sequence showing how they developed from the proposed tool or craft-worker senses.

senses.gloss: achievement, written with 工 for 功
senses.period: bronze inscriptions and Warring States bamboo slip; artifact dates unresolved here
senses.text: In cited contexts 工 is read as 功, ‘achievement’. This is evidence of graphic interchange or borrowing in those contexts, not proof that 工’s work sense developed into achievement.

senses.gloss: tribute or offering, written with 工 for 貢
senses.text: In reported oracle-bone contexts 工 writes 貢. This is a proposed whole-graph sound loan: the sign was reused for a different word because the words were said to sound alike or similar, not because the tool meaning developed into tribute. The early sound match is not independently established by the inspected evidence.

limitations.text: The artifact examples are not dated in the inspected paleographic account, so the senses listed here cannot be arranged into a secure chronology. Current and historical glosses alone do not demonstrate semantic development.

The proposed tool referent, the relation between early official/status uses and later craft/work uses, and the sound basis of the 貢 loan remain unresolved. Close reconstructed readings for 工, 功, and 攻 do not establish a shared semantic history.

overview.text: 工 is a whole-graph picture interpreted as a tool, although the exact object is disputed. Its current senses include work and labor; early uses also include occupations and work, without a demonstrated sequence linking them to the picture.

components.text: Read 工 as one complete picture, proposed to show a tool. The exact object is uncertain; the graph has no separately identified internal components.
